questions.q: After the normalisation step $\hat x_i=(x_i-\mu_B)/\sqrt{\sigma_B^2+\varepsilon}$, why does BatchNorm apply $y_i=\gamma\hat x_i+\beta$ with learnable $\gamma,\beta$?
options: To undo the effect of $\varepsilon$ only
So the network can choose any mean and scale — even recover the original $x$ with $\gamma=\sqrt{\sigma_B^2+\varepsilon}$, $\beta=\mu_B$
To make the output always have mean 0 and variance 1
questions.explain: Forcing every feature to mean 0 / variance 1 could limit what the layer can represent. $\gamma$ and $\beta$ restore that freedom; the page's 'undo' checkbox shows $y=x$ exactly.

questions.q: Inputs have standard deviation $\sigma$. How does the typical fluctuation (standard deviation) of the batch mean $\mu_B$ depend on the batch size $B$?
questions.explain: The mean of $B$ independent samples has variance $\sigma^2/B$. That is why tiny batches give noisy batch statistics and BN struggles with them.

questions.q: At inference time, which statistics does a BatchNorm layer (in eval mode) use?
options: The mean and variance of the current test batch
Running averages of $\mu_B$ and $\sigma_B^2$ collected during training with a momentum update
The statistics of the first training batch
questions.explain: Running estimates $\hat\mu\leftarrow(1-m)\hat\mu+m\,\mu_B$ (and similarly for the variance) make inference deterministic and independent of other examples, even for a single input.

questions.q: For a matrix of activations with rows = examples and columns = features, what does LayerNorm normalise over (compared to BatchNorm)?
options: Each column over the batch, like BatchNorm
Each row over its features — each example on its own, independent of the batch
questions.explain: BatchNorm standardises each feature (column) across the batch; LayerNorm standardises each example (row) across its features, so it works with batch size 1 — one reason transformers use LayerNorm or RMSNorm.
